catalog_quote: East Tusom, like other Tangkhulic languages, has non-contrastive stress that is predictable from weight and morphological factors (which are confounded). There are no stress or weight alternations in our data (but two short syllables sometimes coalesce to form a long syllable). Except in loanwords, morphemes are all monosyllabic (or occasionally, subsyllabic). Roots are simply long (bimoraic) and stressed while prefixes are short (monomoraic) and unstressed. Because this difference is completely predictable, it is not represented in our transcriptions. Only four vowels (/ə/, /i/, /u/, and /ɯ/) occur in unstressed prefix syllables. Suffixes (but not auxiliary verbs, which sometimes have a suffix-like presentation) are short and unstressed as well, as are particles. The general pattern for words in isolation is /LˈH/ (iambic) or—for nominalized verbs with lexical prefixes—/LLˈH/ (anapestic). Examples are show in (1) and (2), respectively: (1) a. ʔì.ˈsí ‘flesh’ b. ʔú.ˈkûə ‘head’ (2) a. kʰə́.ŋə̀ˈlṍ ‘to run’ b. kʰə́.mə́.ˈʑì ‘to accept’ There is no restriction on having multiple stressed syllables (roots) occur contiguously. This is actually quite common in (compound) nouns and verbs.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive. It falls on the root syllable, which is the only long (bimoraic) syllable of the word; the one or two prefix syllables before it (nominalizer, lexical prefix, nasal prefix), any suffix and any particle are short (monomoraic) and unstressed. Since roots are monosyllabic and word-final in simple words, isolation forms are iambic /L'H/ (e.g. ʔì.ˈsí 'flesh', ʔú.ˈkûə 'head') or anapestic /LL'H/ (e.g. kʰə́.ŋə̀ˈlṍ 'to run'); the authors say weight and morphology are confounded, so the pattern can equally be read as 'stress the heavy syllable'. Compounds have as many stressed syllables as roots, with no restriction on contiguous stressed syllables. The language also has three lexical tones (H, L, HL); all three occur on stressed (root) syllables, only H and L on affixes and particles, and HL simplifies to H non-finally.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. The authors state 'There is no restriction on having multiple stressed syllables (roots) occur contiguously. This is actually quite common in (compound) nouns and verbs' (ms. p. 15), i.e. every root in a compound is stressed; no ranking of primary vs secondary stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 6 (p. 14): 'There is at least one exception to this generalization, described below, when the nominalizing prefix occurs before the nasal prefix /N-/' -- the two prefixes coalesce into a single syllable /kʰáN/ (e.g. kʰə-N-tû -> kʰáǹtû 'to meet') whose tone is always H and whose duration is 'considerably longer than that of the nominalizing prefix in other environments' (Table 16, ms. p. 28). Loanwords may have polysyllabic morphemes (e.g. kómbôr 'blanket'). Auxiliary verbs with suffix-like presentation are excluded from the 'suffixes are unstressed' claim. Two short syllables 'sometimes coalesce to form a long syllable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, words in isolation (citation forms) from a 730-item wordlist plus one short text, recorded from one female native speaker in her mid-twenties; instrumental support (Praat/Parselmouth) is given for tone, not for stress. The authors treat stress and vowel length as one 'confounded' property and do not mark it in transcriptions. Prosodic wordhood (relevant to the HL -> H tone rule) 'does not always align neatly with morphological wordhood'.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the speech of the eastern of the two villages named Tusom in Ukhrul district, Manipur ('East Tusom'), as spoken by one consultant; this is exactly Glottolog east2902 (no ISO 639-3 code). It is a distinct Tangkhulic language, not a dialect of Standard Tangkhul/Ukhrul (tang1336): the authors say it differs from Ukhrul 'to a greater degree than German differs from Dutch'. The stress statement is explicitly framed as holding for East Tusom 'like other Tangkhulic languages'.

sources.note: Section 'Stress and Weight' (ms. pp. 14-15): non-contrastive stress predictable from weight and morphology (confounded); roots long (bimoraic) and stressed, prefixes/suffixes/particles short (monomoraic) and unstressed; only /ə i u ɯ/ in unstressed prefix syllables; isolation words are /LˈH/ (iambic) or /LLˈH/ (anapestic); compounds may have several contiguous stressed root syllables. Three tones H, L, HL; HL occurs only on stressed syllables and simplifies to H non-finally.
